title: sed basics
text:
On this page, you use sed to change text: you replace one piece of text with another, delete lines you do not need, and turn a file with another column separator into the tab-separated table. At the end you will use these commands to clean up a file that was saved on Windows and that contains a problem that can quietly break your AWK commands.
Why would you change text with a command, and not by hand? Two jobs come up again and again in biology:
sed does both jobs with one short command, and like AWK, it never changes the file it reads unless you ask for that. You use the same folder as on the last page, with the data in awk_data/.

title: sed basics
section: The shape of a sed command
text:
The shape of a sed command
The command you use most often in sed is s, for substitute (replace):
sed 's/old/new/' file

s tells sed to replace text.
old is the text to look for, and new the text to put in its place. The three slashes / separate the parts.
The part between single quotes is the sed command. Like in AWK, it always goes between single quotes.

sed reads the file one line at a time, makes the change on each line where it finds old, and prints every line, changed or not. For example, to shorten low_P to low:

sed 's/low_P/low/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low mock    ex61    38  6.8
The file itself is not changed. sed only printed a changed version on the screen:

head -3 awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8

title: sed basics
section: The g flag: change every match in a line
text:
The g flag: change every match in a line
Say you want a comma-separated table instead of a tab-separated one. In sed, \t stands for a tab, and you can use this to replace \t with ,:

sed 's/\t/,/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient,Condition  Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P,mock  ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P,mock  ex61    38  6.8
You see that this command didn’t exactly do what you wanted: only the first tab of each line became a comma. That is because by default, s changes only the first match in a line. To change every match, add the flag g (for “global”) after the last slash. A flag is a letter that changes how a command works:

sed 's/\t/,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient,Condition,Experiment,Rootlength,FW_shoot_mg
low_P,mock,ex61,40.4,6.6
low_P,mock,ex61,38,6.8
To check that this worked on the whole file, not only the first lines, count the fields per line with AWK, as on the last page. Since this time the fields are separated by commas, you use -F',':

sed 's/\t/,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | awk -F',' '{ print NF }' | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
    595 5
All 595 lines have 5 fields, so every tab was replaced.






QuestionExercise






Replace mock with control, and look at the first 3 lines of the result.
How many lines contain control after the change (use grep for this task)? Afterwards, confirm the number with AWK: how many lines have mock in column 2 in the original file?







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# 1. Replace and look
sed 's/mock/control/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

# 2. Count after the change, and check with awk on the original file
sed 's/mock/control/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | grep -c 'control'
awk -F'\t' '$2 == "mock"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   control ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   control ex61    38  6.8

209

209
Both give 209, so sed changed exactly the 209 mock plants. mock appears at most once per line, so you do not need the g flag here.

title: sed basics
text:
Special characters: the dot
The text you look for in sed is not plain text, but a regular expression: a pattern in which some characters have a special meaning. Most letters and numbers just mean themselves. But a dot . means “any one character”. See what happens when you try to replace the decimal points with commas:

sed 's/./,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -2

This prints:
,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,
,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,,
You see that every character, letters and tabs included, became a comma. To look for a real dot, you need to put a backslash \ before it in order to take away the special meaning from .:

sed 's/\./,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    40,4    6,6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6,8
You can do a quick sanity check: the number of lines with a comma after the change should equal the number of lines with a dot before. In grep, the dot is special too, so you need the backslash there as well:

sed 's/\./,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | grep -c ','
grep -c '\.' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
590
590
Other characters with a special meaning include *, [, ], ^ and $. You meet $ at the end of this page. If the text you want to replace contains one of them, put a backslash before it.

title: sed basics
section: sed sees the whole line, not columns
text:
sed sees the whole line, not columns
On the last page, grep '13' found 36 more lines than the plants with bacterium 13C, because 13 also appears in numbers such as 13.3. sed has the same problem: it looks for patterns in the whole line, not only in a single column. To test this, replace 13 with X, then count and look at the lines with an X:

sed 's/13/X/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | grep -c 'X'
sed 's/13/X/g' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | grep 'X' | head -3

This prints:
211

low_P   mock    ex61    55.3    X.3
low_P   mock    ex61    48.7    X.9
low_P   mock    ex64    46.93   X.52
211 lines changed, but only 175 plants have bacterium 13C. The first lines with an X are not even 13C plants: they are mock plants whose shoot weight 13.3 became X.3, without any warning. Two ways to avoid this:

Make the text you look for more specific: 13C appears only in column 2.
If the change must happen in one column only, use AWK, which can compare and change a single field.


# More specific text
sed 's/13C/strain13C/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | grep -c 'strain13C'

# Only column 2, with AWK
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '$2 == "13C" { $2 = "strain13C" } { print }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | grep -c 'strain13C'

This prints:
175
175
Both change exactly the 175 lines of the 13C plants.

title: sed basics
text:
Several changes in one command
To make more than one change, separate the s commands with a semicolon ;. sed runs them one after the other, on each line:

sed 's/low_P/low/; s/high_P/high/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
      1 Nutrient
    294 high
    300 low

A file with another column separator
Not every table separates its columns with tabs. The file Growth_Data_dutch.csv holds the same growth data, but with semicolons between the columns and commas as decimal symbol. You may get files like this from a spreadsheet program. That is a key reason to always look at your data first before you do anything with it:

head -3 awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv | cat -A

This prints:
Nutrient;Condition;Experiment;Rootlength;FW_shoot_mg$
low_P;mock;ex61;40,4;6,6$
low_P;mock;ex61;38;6,8$
There is no ^I, so there are no tabs. A file ending in .csv (“comma-separated values”) does not always use commas: always check which character separates the columns before you use the file. Here it is ;, so in AWK you would use -F';':

awk -F';' '{ print NF }' awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
    595 5
If you wanted to turn this file into a tab-separated table with decimal points, you need two changes: commas to dots, and semicolons to tabs.
In the code below, you may wonder why s/,/./g needs no backslash before the dot. The dot is special only in the part you look for, the old part. In the new part, it is just a dot. Here you look for a comma, which has no special meaning, and put a dot in its place.
Save the result in a new file, and check it:

sed 's/,/./g; s/;/\t/g' awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv > Growth_Data_from_csv.txt

# Check: look at it, count the lines and the fields per line
head -3 Growth_Data_from_csv.txt
wc -l Growth_Data_from_csv.txt
awk -F'\t' '{ print NF }' Growth_Data_from_csv.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8

595 Growth_Data_from_csv.txt

    595 5
In this tutorial, you can even check that the result is exactly the original table. cmp compares two files byte by byte. It prints nothing if they are identical, so && echo 'identical' prints a message in that case:

cmp Growth_Data_from_csv.txt awk_data/Growth_Data.txt && echo 'identical'

This prints:
identical






QuestionExercise






Turn Growth_Data_dutch.csv into a real comma-separated file: commas between the columns, and dots as decimal symbol. Check the result with head and with the number of fields per line.
Now swap the order of the two changes in your command. What happens, and why?







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# 1. First the decimal commas to dots, then the semicolons to commas
sed 's/,/./g; s/;/,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv | head -3
sed 's/,/./g; s/;/,/g' awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv | awk -F',' '{ print NF }' | sort | uniq -c

# 2. The other order
sed 's/;/,/g; s/,/./g' awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv | head -3
sed 's/;/,/g; s/,/./g' awk_data/Growth_Data_dutch.csv | awk -F',' '{ print NF }' | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
Nutrient,Condition,Experiment,Rootlength,FW_shoot_mg
low_P,mock,ex61,40.4,6.6
low_P,mock,ex61,38,6.8
    595 5

Nutrient.Condition.Experiment.Rootlength.FW_shoot_mg
low_P.mock.ex61.40.4.6.6
low_P.mock.ex61.38.6.8
    595 1
In the second command, sed first turns the semicolons into commas. The second change then turns all commas into dots, the new column separators included. Each line is now one single field. sed runs the changes in the order you write them, and each change works on the result of the one before.

title: sed basics
text:
Delete lines
Besides s, sed has a command d to delete lines. In front of d, you say which lines you want to delete and you can use a line number, or a pattern between slashes. To delete the header, line 1:

sed '1d' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -2
sed '1d' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8

594
To delete every line that contains high_P, use a pattern (and compare with AWK):

sed '/high_P/d' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' '$1 != "high_P"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
301
301
301 lines: the header and the 300 low_P plants. As with s, sed looks for the pattern in the whole line. Here that is fine, because high_P appears only in column 1.






TipTip: print only some lines with -n and p (optional)





sed prints every line by default. With -n, it prints nothing, unless you ask for it with the command p (print). This is a quick way to look at one line, or a range of lines, by number:

# Line 123, the first plant without a root length
sed -n '123p' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# Lines 2 to 4
sed -n '2,4p' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
high_P  mock    ex61        18.2
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8
low_P   mock    ex61    74.7    8.1
awk 'NR == 123' from the last page does the same.









QuestionExercise






Delete the header and all plants from experiment ex65, with one sed command. How many lines are left? Check the number with AWK.







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Two commands, separated by ;
sed '1d; /ex65/d' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

# Check: rows after the header, where column 3 is not ex65
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $3 != "ex65"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
399
399

title: sed basics
text:
Change a file safely
So far, sed only printed its result, or you saved it in a new file. Sometimes you want to change a file itself, for example to correct a name in a table you keep using. Do this on a copy, never on your original data.
For the rest of this page, you use a second table, mmc5_metadata.txt. It describes 27 bacterial strains, for example their taxonomy and the plant they were isolated from. It comes from a published study, and two of its strains are the bacteria 129E and 13C from the growth data. Later, on the join page, you combine the two tables.
Make a copy, so the file in awk_data/ stays as it is, and look at the strains isolated from legumes. The table has 12 columns, and with cut -f1,6 you only look at the strain name (column 1) and the host plant (column 6):

cp awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt metadata.txt
grep 'Legume' metadata.txt | cut -f1,6

This prints:
USDA61  Legume
R7A Legume
CIAT899 Legume
NGR234  Legume
C58 Legume
The safe way to change a file has three steps: write the result to a new file, check it, and only then replace the old file with the new one. Say you want Legume_host instead of Legume:

# 1. Write the result to a new file
sed 's/Legume/Legume_host/' metadata.txt > metadata_new.txt

# 2. Check: the same number of lines, and only the lines you wanted changed
wc -l metadata.txt metadata_new.txt
diff metadata.txt metadata_new.txt | cut -f1,6

This prints:
  28 metadata.txt
  28 metadata_new.txt
  56 total

4c4
< USDA61    Legume
---
> USDA61    Legume_host
7c7
< R7A   Legume
---
> R7A   Legume_host
10c10
< CIAT899   Legume
---
> CIAT899   Legume_host
17c17
< NGR234    Legume
---
> NGR234    Legume_host
20c20
< C58   Legume
---
> C58   Legume_host
diff compares two files line by line and prints only the lines that differ. 4c4 means: line 4 was changed. Lines starting with < come from the first file, lines starting with > from the second. diff prints whole lines, which are long in this table, so | cut -f1,6 keeps only the strain and the host. Lines such as 4c4 have no tab, and cut prints them as they are. So exactly five lines changed, the way you wanted. Now replace the old file:

# 3. Replace the old file with the new one
mv metadata_new.txt metadata.txt
grep 'Legume' metadata.txt | cut -f1,6

This prints:
USDA61  Legume_host
R7A Legume_host
CIAT899 Legume_host
NGR234  Legume_host
C58 Legume_host

sed -i: change the file itself
sed can also change a file directly, with the option -i (for “in place”). It does the three steps above in one go, but without the check. This is often where mistakes happen. Say you forgot that you already made the change, and run the command again, this time with -i:

sed -i 's/Legume/Legume_host/' metadata.txt
grep 'Legume' metadata.txt | cut -f1,6

This prints:
USDA61  Legume_host_host
R7A Legume_host_host
CIAT899 Legume_host_host
NGR234  Legume_host_host
C58 Legume_host_host
Legume_host still contains Legume, so sed added _host a second time. sed gives no warning, and the old version of the file is gone. This happens easily when you run a script or a notebook a second time.
If you use -i, let sed keep a backup copy. With -i.bak, sed saves the old version as metadata.txt.bak before it changes the file:

sed -i.bak 's/Legume_host_host/Legume_host/' metadata.txt
ls metadata*
grep 'Legume' metadata.txt | cut -f1,6
grep 'Legume' metadata.txt.bak | cut -f1,6

This prints:
metadata.txt
metadata.txt.bak

USDA61  Legume_host
R7A Legume_host
CIAT899 Legume_host
NGR234  Legume_host
C58 Legume_host

USDA61  Legume_host_host
R7A Legume_host_host
CIAT899 Legume_host_host
NGR234  Legume_host_host
C58 Legume_host_host






ImportantBefore you use sed -i




Work on a copy, not on your original data.
If you are not sure, write to a new file first and check it with wc -l and diff.
Ask yourself what happens if the command runs twice. A change like s/Legume/Legume_host/ grows each time, s/Legume_host_host/Legume_host/ does not.









QuestionExercise






Add _host to every host in column 6 of awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt, and save the result in a new file. First look at which hosts there are. Do it once with sed, and once with AWK. Tip: on the AWK page, you glued text together with $1"-"$2.
Check both results: count the values in column 6, and compare the two files.







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Which hosts are there?
cut -f6 awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt | sort | uniq -c

# 1a. sed: one change per host
sed 's/Legume/Legume_host/; s/Arabidopsis/Arabidopsis_host/' awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt > hosts_sed.txt

# 1b. AWK: glue _host to column 6, on every line after the header
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' 'NR > 1 { $6 = $6 "_host" } { print }' awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt > hosts_awk.txt

# 2. Check
cut -f6 hosts_sed.txt | sort | uniq -c
cut -f6 hosts_awk.txt | sort | uniq -c
cmp hosts_sed.txt hosts_awk.txt && echo 'identical'

This prints:
     22 Arabidopsis
      5 Legume
      1 host

     22 Arabidopsis_host
      5 Legume_host
      1 host

     22 Arabidopsis_host
      5 Legume_host
      1 host

identical
Both commands give the same file, and most strains turn out to come from Arabidopsis, like the plants in the growth data. The sed version works here because you looked first: there are only two hosts, and these two words appear nowhere else in the table. With many different hosts, you would need one change for each.
The AWK version changes column 6 on every line, whatever is in it. $6 "_host" glues the text _host to the value in column 6. Three mistakes give a wrong result without an error:

Without NR > 1, the header becomes host_host.
Run the command a second time, on hosts_awk.txt, and you get Arabidopsis_host_host, as with sed -i above.
Without the double quotes around _host, AWK reads _host as the name of an empty variable, and nothing changes.













TipTip: sed on a Mac (optional)






The sed on a Mac is a different version (BSD sed). Two differences matter for this page: sed -i needs a backup ending after it (sed -i '' ... for no backup, or sed -i.bak ...), and \t may not mean a tab in the text you look for. If a command from this page does not work on your Mac, this is a likely reason.

title: sed basics
text:
Windows line endings
Every line in a text file ends with an invisible character that says “a new line starts here”. Linux and Mac use one character for this, written as \n. Windows uses two: \r\n. A table saved on Windows, for example from Excel, may therefore have a hidden \r at the end of every line. You do not see it on screen, but AWK and grep on Linux see it as part of the last column and this can create silent errors that you will only catch if you closely inspect the output of your commands.
The metadata table you use below was saved from Excel on a Windows PC. file tells you what kind of text a file holds. Compare it with the growth data:

file awk_data/Growth_Data.txt awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt

This prints:
awk_data/Growth_Data.txt:   ASCII text
awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt: ASCII text, with CRLF line terminators
CRLF is the name for the Windows line ending \r\n. Now see what it does. Column 12, the last column, holds TRUE, FALSE or NA. Count these values with the tools from the CLI workshop, and then let AWK count the rows with TRUE:

cut -f12 awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt | sort | uniq -c
awk -F'\t' '$12 == "TRUE"' awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt | wc -l

This prints:
      1 Colonization
      3 FALSE
     13 NA
     11 TRUE

0
cut shows 11 rows with TRUE, but AWK finds 0, and there is no error. That happens because column 12 is TRUE\r, not TRUE and therefore the AWK pattern matches nothing. The problem for you is that \r is invisible on screen, also in the output of cut above. You can use cat -A, which shows the Windows line ending as ^M. Since column 12 is the last column you can use cut -f1,12 to have a short view of the strain name and the line end:

head -3 awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt | cut -f1,12
head -3 awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt | cut -f1,12 | cat -A

This prints:
strain  Colonization
Root123D2   NA
Root381 NA

strain^IColonization^M$
Root123D2^INA^M$
Root381^INA^M$

Remove the \r with sed
To remove the \r, replace it with nothing. In sed, \r stands for this character, and $ means “the end of the line”. So s/\r$// removes a \r only where it sits at the end of a line:

sed 's/\r$//' awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt > mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt

# Check: file type, the hidden characters, the number of lines and characters,
# and the count from before
file mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt
head -3 mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | cut -f1,12 | cat -A
wc -l mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt
wc -c awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt
awk -F'\t' '$12 == "TRUE"' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | wc -l

This prints:
mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt: ASCII text

strain^IColonization$
Root123D2^INA$
Root381^INA$

28 mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt

2808 awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt
2780 mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt
5588 total

11
The ^M is gone, and AWK finds the 11 rows. wc -c counts characters: the fixed file has 28 lines and 28 characters fewer, one \r per line. Keep mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt, you use it on the next page.






ImportantGit Bash hides this problem



The outputs on this page come from Linux (Ubuntu in WSL). In Git Bash on Windows, AWK and grep ignore the \r: they find 11 rows with TRUE also in the original file. The file still has the \r, though, and file, cat -A and sed show it in Git Bash too. As soon as you use the file on Linux, for example on a computer cluster, the problem appears. So check new files with file or cat -A, whatever system you work on.








TipTip: remove the \r with tr (optional)





You will often see another command for the same job: tr -d '\r' deletes every \r in a file. tr reads only from a pipe or with <, not from a file name:

tr -d '\r' < awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt > mmc5_metadata_fixed_tr.txt
cmp mmc5_metadata_fixed_tr.txt mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt && echo 'identical'

This prints:
identical
Both commands give the same result here.

title: sed basics
text:
What you learned

sed 's/old/new/' file replaces the first match in each line, s/old/new/g every match.
The text you look for is a regular expression: . means any character, \. a real dot. \t is a tab, \r the hidden Windows character, $ the end of a line.
sed looks at the whole line, not at columns. Make the text you look for specific, or use AWK to change one column.
Separate several changes with ;. They run in the order you write them.
sed '1d' deletes line 1, sed '/text/d' every line that contains text.
Check which character separates the columns before you use a file, also when it ends in .csv.
Change a file safely: work on a copy, write to a new file, check with wc -l and diff, then replace. With sed -i, keep a backup (-i.bak), and think about what happens if the command runs twice.
Windows line endings (\r, ^M in cat -A) make text matches on the last column fail without an error. Find them with file or cat -A, and remove them with sed 's/\r$//'.

On the next page, More useful AWK, you learn a few more AWK forms that are handy in your own work and common in code from an LLM.

title: More useful AWK
text:
This page adds a few AWK forms that you will find useful in your own work: change text in one column, search one column for a pattern, give AWK a value from outside, for example in a loop over files, and split a value into parts. You will also see these forms often in commands from an LLM or a forum, so after this page you can read them too. You do not need to write them from memory. The goal is that you know what they do, when they are handy, and how to check the result.
You use the same folder as on the previous pages, with awk_data/Growth_Data.txt and mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt, the strain metadata without Windows line endings from the sed page. If you do not have it anymore, make it again:
sed 's/\r$//' awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt > mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt

title: More useful AWK
text:
Rename two strains
The growth data and the strain metadata describe the same two bacteria, but with different names: 129E and 13C in the growth data, R129_E and R13_C in column 1 of the metadata. On the next page you combine the two tables, and for that the names must match. Here is a command that renames the two strains in the metadata, of the kind you get from an LLM or a forum:

awk 'BEGIN{FS=OFS="\t"} {gsub(/R129_E/, "129E", $1); gsub(/R13_C/, "13C", $1); print}' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt > mmc5_metadata_awk.txt

# Check: the number of lines, and which lines changed
wc -l mmc5_metadata_awk.txt
diff mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt mmc5_metadata_awk.txt | cut -f1,4

# The same change with sed, and a comparison
sed 's/^R129_E/129E/; s/^R13_C/13C/' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt > mmc5_metadata_named.txt
cmp mmc5_metadata_awk.txt mmc5_metadata_named.txt && echo 'identical'

This prints:
28 mmc5_metadata_awk.txt

11c11
< R129_E    Rhizobium
---
> 129E  Rhizobium
14c14
< R13_C Rhizobium
---
> 13C   Rhizobium

identical
The command works: only lines 11 and 14 changed, and the file is the same as the one from sed. In the sed command, ^ means “the start of the line”, so sed only changes a name that stands at the start of a line, in column 1. Keep mmc5_metadata_named.txt, you use it on the next page.
The AWK command uses two forms you have not seen yet: BEGIN{FS=OFS="\t"} and gsub(...). The next two sections take them apart.

title: More useful AWK
text:
BEGIN: before the first line
BEGIN is a pattern, like NR == 1. Its action runs once, before AWK reads the first line. It is the opposite of END, which you know from the AWK page: that action runs once, after the last line. You can see both in a small test:

awk 'BEGIN { print "start" } END { print "end, lines read:", NR }' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt

This prints:
start
end, lines read: 28
BEGIN is a good place for settings that must be ready before the first line is read. FS is the field separator, the same setting that -F gives. OFS is the output field separator, the one you set with -v OFS='\t'. FS=OFS="\t" sets both to a tab in one go. So these two commands do the same:

awk 'BEGIN{FS=OFS="\t"} {gsub(/R129_E/, "129E", $1); gsub(/R13_C/, "13C", $1); print}' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt > mmc5_metadata_awk.txt

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '{gsub(/R129_E/, "129E", $1); gsub(/R13_C/, "13C", $1); print}' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt > mmc5_metadata_awk2.txt

cmp mmc5_metadata_awk2.txt mmc5_metadata_awk.txt && echo 'identical'

This prints:
identical
Which form you use is a matter of taste. LLMs often write the BEGIN form.






ImportantForget OFS, and only the changed lines break



If you set only FS and leave out OFS, AWK uses a space between the columns of each line it changed. Lines without a change stay as they are:

awk 'BEGIN{FS="\t"} {gsub(/R129_E/, "129E", $1); gsub(/R13_C/, "13C", $1); print}' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt > mmc5_metadata_noofs.txt

# Look at line 10 (not changed) and line 11 (changed), and count the fields per line
sed -n '10,11p' mmc5_metadata_noofs.txt | cat -A
awk -F'\t' '{ print NF }' mmc5_metadata_noofs.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
CIAT899^IRhizobiales^IRhizobiaceae^IRhizobium^INodule^ILegume^ITRUE^IRhizobium spp.^I2^ITY^ITRUE^INA$
129E Rhizobiales Rhizobiaceae Rhizobium Root Arabidopsis FALSE Rhizobium spp. 2 TY TRUE TRUE$

      2 1
     26 12
Line 10 still has tabs (^I), line 11 has spaces. For a tab-separated file, line 11 is now one long field. Only the 2 renamed lines broke, so head would show you nothing wrong. Counting the fields per line shows it. When you read a command that changes a column, look for OFS.

title: More useful AWK
section: sub and gsub: replace text in a field
text:
sub and gsub: replace text in a field
gsub(/R129_E/, "129E", $1) means: in column 1, replace every match of R129_E with 129E. It is AWK’s version of sed’s s/R129_E/129E/g, but limited to one field. The three parts are:

/R129_E/: what to look for, a regular expression between slashes, as in sed.
"129E": the replacement, in double quotes.
$1: where to look. Without it, AWK looks in the whole line.

sub works the same, but replaces only the first match, like sed’s s without g. You can see the difference on the header of the metadata, where two column names contain a space. Many tools, R among them, are easier to use with column names without spaces:

head -1 mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt
awk 'NR == 1 { sub(/ /, "_") } { print }' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | head -1
awk 'NR == 1 { gsub(/ /, "_") } { print }' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | head -1

This prints:
strain  Order   Family  Genus   compartment host    nifH    Taxonomy group  optimal dpi Media   RGP Colonization

strain  Order   Family  Genus   compartment host    nifH    Taxonomy_group  optimal dpi Media   RGP Colonization

strain  Order   Family  Genus   compartment host    nifH    Taxonomy_group  optimal_dpi Media   RGP Colonization
sub changed only the first space, gsub both. Here neither has a field after the regular expression, so they work on the whole line. The pattern NR == 1 limits the change to the header: the values Rhizobium spp. and 50% TSB further down keep their spaces. Check that with diff:

awk 'NR == 1 { gsub(/ /, "_") } { print }' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt > mmc5_metadata_header.txt

wc -l mmc5_metadata_header.txt
diff mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt mmc5_metadata_header.txt

This prints:
28 mmc5_metadata_header.txt

1c1
< strain    Order   Family  Genus   compartment host    nifH    Taxonomy group  optimal dpi Media   RGP Colonization
---
> strain    Order   Family  Genus   compartment host    nifH    Taxonomy_group  optimal_dpi Media   RGP Colonization
Only line 1 changed.

title: More useful AWK
section: ~ and !~: match a pattern in one field
text:
~ and !~: match a pattern in one field
So far, you kept lines with ==, which means “exactly equal”. ~ means “contains a match of this regular expression”, and !~ means “does not contain a match”. Look at column 8, the taxonomy group:

awk -F'\t' '$8 == "Rhizobium"' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' '$8 ~ /Rhizobium/' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | cut -f1,8

This prints:
0

CIAT899 Rhizobium spp.
R129_E  Rhizobium spp.
R129_N  Rhizobium spp.
R13_A   Rhizobium spp.
R13_C   Rhizobium spp.
Rg  Rhizobium spp.
Root149 Rhizobium spp.
No value in column 8 is exactly Rhizobium, so == finds nothing. ~ finds the 7 lines in which column 8 contains Rhizobium. The difference with grep Rhizobium is that grep looks in the whole line, and ~ only in the column you name. Here Rhizobium is also a genus in column 4, so with grep you could not tell which column matched.
The special characters from sed work here too, for example ^ for the start. $1 ~ /^Root/ keeps the strains whose name starts with Root:

awk -F'\t' '$1 ~ /^Root/' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | wc -l

This prints:
17
With !~, you can look for values that do not have the form you expect. A root length should be a number: only digits and a decimal point. In a regular expression, [0-9.] means “one character that is a digit or a dot”, and + means “the character before it, once or more”. So ^[0-9.]+$ means “from start to end only digits and dots”. Look for the lines where column 4 is not like that:

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 !~ /^[0-9.]+$/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 !~ /^[0-9.]+$/' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3 | cat -A

This prints:
15

high_P^Imock^Iex61^I^I18.2$
high_P^Imock^Iex64^I^I22.4$
high_P^Imock^Iex64^I^I26$
These are the 15 plants without a root length from the AWK page: an empty field is not a number either. In a new table, this check also finds values such as NA, 12,5 or 12 mm.






QuestionExercise





On the sed page, you added _host to every host in column 6 with NR > 1 { $6 = $6 "_host" }. Run twice, that command gives Arabidopsis_host_host. Change it, so that it adds _host only to hosts that do not end in _host yet. Use mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt, save the result as metadata_host.txt, then run your command a second time on metadata_host.txt and check that nothing changes.






AnswerClick me to see an answer





Add $6 !~ /_host$/ to the pattern. _host$ means “_host at the end”, and !~ means “does not match”:

# Run once, and a second time on the result
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' 'NR > 1 && $6 !~ /_host$/ { $6 = $6 "_host" } { print }' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt > metadata_host.txt

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' 'NR > 1 && $6 !~ /_host$/ { $6 = $6 "_host" } { print }' metadata_host.txt > metadata_host2.txt

# Check
cut -f6 metadata_host2.txt | sort | uniq -c
cmp metadata_host.txt metadata_host2.txt && echo 'identical'

This prints:
     22 Arabidopsis_host
      5 Legume_host
      1 host

identical
The second run changed nothing. A command that you can safely run twice is worth a lot in a script or a notebook that you run again later.

title: More useful AWK
section: -v: give AWK a value from outside
text:
-v: give AWK a value from outside
You know -v from -v OFS='\t': it sets a variable before AWK starts. A variable is a name that holds a value. You can make your own, with any name you like. Here strain holds the text 129E:

awk -F'\t' -v strain=129E '$2 == strain' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' -v strain=13C '$2 == strain' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
210
175
Inside the AWK command, strain has no quotes: it is the name of the variable, not the text strain. The command stays the same, and only the value after -v changes.
This is most useful in a for loop in bash, which repeats a command for each value in a list. In the loop below, the bash variable s holds 129E, then 13C, then mock. -v strain="$s" hands each value over to AWK, and AWK writes one file per condition, with the header (NR == 1):

for s in 129E 13C mock; do
  awk -F'\t' -v strain="$s" 'NR == 1 || $2 == strain' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > growth_"$s".txt
done

# Check
wc -l growth_129E.txt growth_13C.txt growth_mock.txt
head -2 growth_13C.txt
cut -f2 growth_13C.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
  211 growth_129E.txt
  176 growth_13C.txt
  210 growth_mock.txt
  597 total

Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   13C ex61    54.3    1.56

    175 13C
      1 Condition
Each file has its plants plus the header line: 210 + 175 + 209 plants, plus 3 headers, is 597.






ImportantA bash variable inside single quotes stays text



Why not write $s straight into the AWK command? Bash does not look inside single quotes, so AWK gets the text $s and not the value. Try it:

for s in 129E 13C mock; do
  echo "$s"
  awk -F'\t' '$2 == "$s"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
done

This prints:
129E
0
13C
0
mock
0
The loop runs, s holds the right value, but AWK finds 0 lines each time, without an error. AWK looked for plants with the condition $s, and there are none. Use -v to pass a bash variable to AWK.

title: More useful AWK
section: split: cut a value into parts
text:
split: cut a value into parts
split cuts a value into parts at a separator, and puts the parts in an array. Here the names in the array are numbers: parts[1] is the first part, parts[2] the second, and so on. It gives back the number of parts. Take the four strain names with an underscore:

awk -F'\t' '$1 ~ /_/ { n = split($1, parts, "_"); print $1, n, parts[1], parts[2] }' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt

This prints:
R129_E 2 R129 E
R129_N 2 R129 N
R13_A 2 R13 A
R13_C 2 R13 C
split($1, parts, "_") means: cut column 1 at each _, and put the pieces in parts. R129_E gives 2 parts, R129 and E. The number of parts is a useful check. For example, split the taxonomy group in column 8 at the space, and count how many words each value has:

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 { n = split($8, words, " "); print n, $8 }' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
      2 1 Agrobacterium
      3 1 Bradyrhizobium
      3 1 Caulobacterales
      2 1 Hyphomicrobiaceae
      3 1 Mesorhizobium
      3 1 Sinorhizobium
      4 1 Sphingomonadales
      7 2 Rhizobium spp.
All values are one word, except Rhizobium spp. with two. You see split often in commands that take apart names like sample_rep1_R1, or a column with values such as Bacteria;Proteobacteria;Alphaproteobacteria.






TipTip: one general rule for all names, with capture groups (optional)





The command at the top of this page uses one explicit change per name. A quick general rule, such as “remove the R at the start and the underscore”, would also turn Root123D2 into oot123D2. A general rule can work, if it is precise and you check what it changes. sed can remember parts of a match with capture groups: the parts of a regular expression between brackets ( ). In the replacement, \1 puts back what the first pair of brackets matched, and \2 the second:

sed -E 's/^R([0-9]+)_([A-Z])\t/\1\2\t/' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt > mmc5_metadata_regex.txt

# Check
wc -l mmc5_metadata_regex.txt
diff mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt mmc5_metadata_regex.txt | cut -f1
cut -f1 mmc5_metadata_regex.txt | grep -c '^oot'

This prints:
28 mmc5_metadata_regex.txt

11,14c11,14
< R129_E
< R129_N
< R13_A
< R13_C
---
> 129E
> 129N
> 13A
> 13C

0
Read the regular expression from left to right: ^R an R at the start of the line, ([0-9]+) one or more digits (group 1), _ an underscore, ([A-Z]) one capital letter (group 2), and \t the tab at the end of column 1. -E tells sed that brackets mean capture groups. (Tested with GNU sed. On a Mac, see the tip about \t on the sed page.) So R129_E becomes 129E, and Root123D2 does not match, because an o is not a digit. The last check counts the names that start with oot: 0.
The rule changed four names, not only the two in the growth data. That is fine here, because all four now follow the same naming scheme. The diff shows you exactly which names changed, so you can decide. A rename with split and sub gives an identical file.
In code from an LLM, you may also see match($1, /^R([0-9]+)_([A-Z])$/, m), which puts the groups in the array m. This only works in GNU awk: run with gawk --posix, AWK stops with “match: third argument is a gawk extension”. (Tested 2026-10-29 in WSL and Git Bash. Not tested on a Mac.)

title: More useful AWK
text:
What you learned

BEGIN { ... } runs before the first line, END { ... } after the last. BEGIN{FS=OFS="\t"} does the same as -F'\t' -v OFS='\t'.
Without OFS, only the lines that AWK changed lose their tabs. Count the fields per line to find this.
gsub(/old/, "new", $1) replaces every match in column 1, sub only the first. Without a field, they work on the whole line.
$8 ~ /text/ keeps lines where column 8 contains a match, $8 !~ /text/ the other lines. == needs an exact match.
!~ with a pattern such as /^[0-9.]+$/ finds values that do not have the form you expect.
-v name=value gives AWK a value from outside. Use it to pass a bash variable into AWK: $s inside single quotes stays text.
split(value, parts, "_") cuts a value into parts, and gives back how many there are.
A general rename can work if it is precise. Check with diff which names it changed.

On the next page, Combining two files, you add the genus from the strain metadata to the growth data.

title: Welcome
text:
This tutorial shows you how to work with tables and other text files on the command line with two small tools: AWK and sed. You can use these tools to select rows and columns, to calculate sums and means, to clean up names, and to combine information from two files. You will try every command on real biological data: a table with plant growth measurements, and a table with information on the bacterial strains used in that experiment.
Important: This tutorial is still work in progress, missing chapters will be added over time

title: Welcome
text:
What are AWK and sed?
AWK is a small programming language made for tables. It reads a file one line at a time and splits each line into fields, the separate values in a line, like the cells in one row of a spreadsheet. You then tell AWK what to do with these fields, for example “print the second and fourth column” or “keep only the rows where the root length is above 50”.
sed (short for “stream editor”) reads a file one line at a time and changes the text on the fly. You use it mostly to search and replace, for example to shorten a long sequence name, or to delete lines you do not need.
Both tools come with almost every Linux and Mac system, they work on files of any size, and they need only one line of code for many everyday tasks. That is why you meet them in many bioinformatics scripts and tutorials.

title: Welcome
section: Why not just use Excel, R or Python?
text:
Why not just use Excel, R or Python?
For statistics and plots, R or Python are the better tools. But for many smaller jobs, AWK and sed have some real advantages:

You keep a record of what you did. A command can be saved in a script or a notebook, and run again on new data. A table that you change by hand in Excel leaves no record, and Excel sometimes changes your data without asking: it is known to turn gene names such as SEPT2 into dates.
The same step works on many files. Together with a for loop, one command can clean the names in 50 FASTA files, or take one column from 200 sample tables.
Nothing to install. AWK and sed are already on your computer and on most computer clusters, so you do not need packages or extra software.

title: Welcome
section: Why learn this when an LLM can write it?
text:
Why learn this when an LLM can write it?
LLMs (large language models, such as ChatGPT or Claude) are normally good at writing AWK and sed commands. So it is not the goal of this tutorial to make you write long AWK programs from memory. Instead, after this tutorial you should be able to:

read a short AWK or sed command, and say what it does
check whether it does what you asked for, on your own data
adapt it, for example to use another column or another file
recognize the common traps, where a command runs without an error but gives the wrong result

The last point matters most. A command that fails with an error message is easy to notice. A command that quietly skips a few rows, or treats a missing value as a zero, is not.

title: Welcome
text:
What you will do

Use AWK on a table: print and select columns and rows, add a column, and calculate counts and means per group
Learn sed basics: search and replace text, delete lines, change a file safely, and remove Windows line endings
Use more of AWK: change text in one column (gsub), search one column (~), pass a value into AWK (-v), split a value into parts (split), and read BEGIN, which you see often in code from an LLM or a forum
Combine two files: add information from the strain table to the growth data, make names match, and check the result
Use AWK and sed on FASTA files (optional): count sequences and clean up sequence names (in planning)
Check code from an LLM: a short routine to test any AWK or sed command before you trust its output (in planning)

title: Welcome
text:
Before you start
To follow this tutorial you need:

A terminal and the command line basics. This tutorial assumes you have worked through the basics of the CLI workshop: moving around with cd and ls, looking at files with head and wc, and combining commands with a pipe (|). It also helps if you have used grep and cut. If you have never opened a terminal, start with Before you start of the CLI workshop.
Your own computer. All commands are meant to run on your laptop. If you already know how to use Crunchomics, the UvA computer cluster, you can also work there (see the HPC pages of the CLI workshop).
The example data. You download it at the start of the first page, with two commands. It is small (about 14 kB), so it fits on any laptop. The data comes from an experiment where Arabidopsis plants grew with low or high phosphorus, either without bacteria or inoculated with one of two rhizobia strains. For each plant, root length and shoot weight were measured. The question was whether these bacteria promote plant growth, and might help plants grow when nutrients are limited. A second table describes these and other strains, from a published study.







ImportantAWK and sed are not the same on every computer



There are several versions of AWK and sed. Linux systems and Crunchomics usually have the GNU versions, Macs have different (BSD) versions, and the terminal in MobaXterm may have yet another one. Most commands in this tutorial work everywhere, and where a command behaves differently, the page says so. 


Start with AWK on a table.

title: Combining two files
text:
On this page, you add information from one table to another: the genus of each bacterial strain, from the strain metadata, to each plant in the growth data. Combining two tables by a shared name is called a join. It is one of the most common jobs in bioinformatics, for example when you add sample information to a table of read counts, or a taxonomy to a list of sequences. It is also a job where small mistakes give a wrong result without any error message, so a large part of this page is about checking the result.
You use the same folder as on the previous pages. You need two files: awk_data/Growth_Data.txt, and mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt, the strain metadata without Windows line endings that you made at the end of the sed page. If you do not have it anymore, make it again:
sed 's/\r$//' awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt > mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt

title: Combining two files
text:
Look at both files first
The metadata table has 12 columns. Look at the first six, and count the fields per line:

head -3 mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | cut -f1-6
awk -F'\t' '{ print NF }' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
strain  Order   Family  Genus   compartment host
Root123D2   Rhizobiales Bradyrhizobiaceae   Afipia  Root    Arabidopsis
Root381 Rhizobiales Bradyrhizobiaceae   Bosea   Root    Arabidopsis

     28 12
Each line describes one strain, and all 28 lines (the header and 27 strains) have 12 fields. Column 1 is the name of the strain, column 4 its genus.

Why -F'\t' matters here too
Some values in this table contain a space, for example the medium 50% TSB or the column name Taxonomy group. Check what happens if you don’t use -F'\t', and see how AWK splits the lines at these spaces:

awk '{ print NF }' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
     15 12
     12 13
      1 14
You see that 13 lines now have more than 12 fields, so the NF check shows that something is off.
But the 15 lines with 12 fields are not all right either. If you open the table in a spreadsheet program such as Excel, you see three strains with an empty cell in the Genus column: Root154, Root700 and Root77. All three grew on 50% TSB, a value with a space. You can also find the empty cells with a command, as on the AWK page:

awk -F'\t' '$4 == ""' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | cut -f1,4,10

This prints:
Root154     50% TSB
Root700     50% TSB
Root77      50% TSB
Without -F'\t', that line loses one field (the empty genus) and gains one (the space in 50% TSB), so the count looks fine while the table itself is actually not what you want:

awk -F'\t' '$1 == "Root154" { print $4 }' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt
awk '$1 == "Root154" { print $4 }' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt

This prints:

Root
With -F'\t', column 4 of Root154 is empty, which is correct. Without it, column 4 is Root, the value from column 5. So always set the field separator, also when a table looks simple.


The names in both files
The two tables share the names of the bacteria: column 2 of the growth data, and column 1 of the metadata. First look at the names in the growth data. Then search the metadata for the numbers of these two bacteria, 129 and 13:

# The bacteria names in the growth data
cut -f2 awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | sort | uniq -c

# Names in the metadata that contain 129 or 13
cut -f1 mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | grep '129'
cut -f1 mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | grep '13'

This prints:
    210 129E
    175 13C
      1 Condition
    209 mock

R129_E
R129_N

R13_A
R13_C
You can see that bacteria 129E and 13C are the names used in the growth data, but in the metadata these bacteria are called R129_E and R13_C. These are the same strains, written in two ways. AWK compares names letter by letter, so 129E and R129_E do not match. Before you can combine the tables, the names must be the same.

title: Combining two files
text:
Make the names match
This happens all the time: one person writes Sample-01, another Sample_01, and the sequencing center sends back S01. A good habit is to choose one way of naming your samples at the start of a project, for example short names without spaces or special characters, and to use it everywhere: in your lab notes, in file names and in every table. Fixing names afterwards is extra work, and it is easy to get wrong.
Here you change the names in the metadata, the smaller of the two tables. You need to change two names, so it is best to write the two changes out. The ^ means “the start of the line”, as on the page More useful AWK. It makes sure that sed changes a name only at the start of a line, in column 1:

sed 's/^R129_E/129E/; s/^R13_C/13C/' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt > mmc5_metadata_named.txt

# Check: the same number of lines, and only the lines you wanted changed
wc -l mmc5_metadata_named.txt
diff mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt mmc5_metadata_named.txt | cut -f1,4

This prints:
28 mmc5_metadata_named.txt

11c11
< R129_E    Rhizobium
---
> 129E  Rhizobium
14c14
< R13_C Rhizobium
---
> 13C   Rhizobium
You see that exactly two lines changed. If you made mmc5_metadata_named.txt on the previous page, this gives the same file: there, an AWK command did the same rename with gsub, and the result was identical. This also shows a good habit: whenever you use a command to change names, check it as above: look at all names after the change, not only at the ones you wanted to change.






TipTip: why not one general rule? (optional)





Another idea to change names is to change all names at once, for example: remove the R at the start, and the underscore. ^R means “an R at the start of the line”:

cut -f1 mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | sed 's/^R//; s/_//' | grep '^1'
cut -f1 mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt | sed 's/^R//; s/_//' | head -4

This prints:
129E
129N
13A
13C

strain
oot123D2
oot381
USDA61
129E and 13C look right now, and a join would work. But every strain whose name starts with Root lost its R too: 17 strains are now called oot.... A general rule works for the names you had in mind, but it is easy to forget what it does to the other names in the file. You only notice this if you look at the other names as well.

title: Combining two files
text:
Add the genus: NR == FNR






NoteThe most advanced part of this tutorial



Combining two files with AWK is harder than anything before it. If it does not make sense on the first read, that is normal: take your time, and run each step yourself. What matters most is that you recognize the NR == FNR pattern when you see it, for example in code from an LLM, and that you know the checks in “Check the result” below. These checks work no matter which command did the combining.


AWK can read two files, one after the other. The command below first reads the metadata and remembers the genus of each strain. Then it reads the growth data and adds the remembered genus to each line:

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  NR == FNR  { genus[$1] = $4; next }
             { print $0, genus[$2] }
' mmc5_metadata_named.txt awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > growth_genus.txt

# Check
wc -l growth_genus.txt
head -3 growth_genus.txt
awk -F'\t' '$2 == "129E"' growth_genus.txt | head -2
awk -F'\t' '$2 == "13C"' growth_genus.txt | head -2

This prints:
595 growth_genus.txt

Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8

low_P   129E    ex61    86.1    5.5 Rhizobium
low_P   129E    ex61    58.4    7.5 Rhizobium

low_P   13C ex61    54.3    1.56    Rhizobium
low_P   13C ex61    81  4   Rhizobium
595 lines, as many as in the growth data. The plants with 129E and 13C now have Rhizobium in a new column 6. The mock plants have an empty column 6, because no strain is called mock. You will see NR == FNR in many AWK commands that combine two files, so it is worth taking it apart.
The command has two parts, each with its own pattern and action: NR == FNR { genus[$1] = $4; next } and { print $0, genus[$2] }. For each line, AWK checks the parts from top to bottom, and runs the action of every part whose pattern matches. A part without a pattern runs on every line. next stops this: AWK skips the remaining parts and goes on to the next line. Below, you look at each piece in turn.
NR and FNR. You know NR from the AWK page: the line number. When AWK reads several files, NR keeps counting across all of them. FNR is the line number within the current file, and starts at 1 again in each new file. FILENAME holds the name of the current file. You can see the difference where AWK moves from the first file to the second (sed -n '27,30p' prints lines 27 to 30):

awk '{ print FILENAME, NR, FNR }' mmc5_metadata_named.txt awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | sed -n '27,30p'

This prints:
mmc5_metadata_named.txt 27 27
mmc5_metadata_named.txt 28 28
awk_data/Growth_Data.txt 29 1
awk_data/Growth_Data.txt 30 2
In the first file, NR and FNR are the same. From the second file on, they differ. So the pattern NR == FNR is true only while AWK reads the first file.
The first part, NR == FNR { genus[$1] = $4; next }, therefore runs only on the metadata. Here, genus is an array, a variable that holds one value per name, as on the AWK page. Take line 11 of the metadata, now that you renamed the strain:
129E    Rhizobiales Rhizobiaceae    Rhizobium   Root    Arabidopsis FALSE   Rhizobium spp.  2   TY  TRUE    TRUE
Here $1 is 129E and $4 is Rhizobium. So genus[$1] = $4 means genus["129E"] = "Rhizobium": store the genus from column 4 under the name of the strain in column 1. You use the strain as the name, because the strain is what you want to look up later in the growth data. The genus is the value, because that is what you want back. Then next makes AWK go on to the next line, so the second part does not run on the metadata.
You can look at the values in the array after AWK has read the whole metadata table:

awk -F'\t' '
  { genus[$1] = $4 }
  END {
    print "129E:", genus["129E"]
    print "Root154:", genus["Root154"]
    print "mock:", genus["mock"]
  }
' mmc5_metadata_named.txt

This prints:
129E: Rhizobium
Root154:
mock:
Root154 has an empty value, because this strain has no genus in the table. mock is not in the array at all, and AWK gives you empty text for it, without an error. In the result, both look the same: an empty field.
The second part, { print $0, genus[$2] }, has no pattern, so it runs on every line that gets this far: only the lines of the growth data. Take this line:
low_P   129E    ex61    86.1    5.5
Now $2 is the strain, 129E, because in the growth data the strain is in column 2. So genus[$2] is genus["129E"], the value stored in the first part, and AWK prints:
low_P   129E    ex61    86.1    5.5 Rhizobium
Note that $1, $2 and so on always mean the columns of the line AWK is reading at that moment. In the metadata, the strain is $1 and the genus $4. In the growth data, the strain is $2. So you choose the column numbers for each file separately.
The order of the files matters. The table you look things up in comes first, the table you add to comes second. If you swap them, AWK remembers the growth data and adds a column to the metadata instead. The result has 28 lines, and the new column is empty on every line. AWK gives no error, but a quick wc -l shows that something is wrong: you expected 595 lines.

Give the new column a name
The result has the right number of lines, but it is not finished yet. Look at the end of the first two lines with cat -A:

head -2 growth_genus.txt | cat -A

This prints:
Nutrient^ICondition^IExperiment^IRootlength^IFW_shoot_mg^I$
low_P^Imock^Iex61^I40.4^I6.6^I$
Both lines end with a tab and nothing after it: an empty column 6. For the mock plant, that is expected. For the header it is not: the new column has no name. The header went through the second part like any other line. Column 2 of the header is Condition, and Condition is not a name in the array.
To give the new column a name, add a new part between the two others. Its pattern, FNR == 1, matches line 1 of a file. The metadata never gets this far, because the first part skips every metadata line to the next line with next. So the new part only runs on the header of the growth data:

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  NR == FNR  { genus[$1] = $4; next }
  FNR == 1   { print $0, "Genus"; next }
             { print $0, genus[$2] }
' mmc5_metadata_named.txt awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > growth_genus.txt

# Check
wc -l growth_genus.txt
head -3 growth_genus.txt

This prints:
595 growth_genus.txt

Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg Genus
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8
The new part also ends with next. It makes sure that the header is not printed a second time by the last part, { print $0, genus[$2] }.






ImportantForget next, and the first file ends up in the result



Without next in the first part, the other parts also run on the lines of the metadata. You get no error:

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  NR == FNR  { genus[$1] = $4 }
  FNR == 1   { print $0, "Genus"; next }
             { print $0, genus[$2] }
' mmc5_metadata_named.txt awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > growth_genus_nonext.txt

wc -l growth_genus_nonext.txt
head -3 growth_genus_nonext.txt | cut -f1,13

This prints:
623 growth_genus_nonext.txt

strain  Genus
Root123D2
Root381
You get 623 lines instead of 595: first the 28 lines of the metadata, each with an extra column, and then the 595 lines you wanted. (cut -f1,13 shows the strain and column 13, the new column after the 12 columns of the metadata.) The line count shows the problem right away.

title: Combining two files
text:
Check the result
The line count tells you that no lines were lost or added. It does not tell you whether each line got the right genus. Two more checks help.
Check 1: lines without a genus. Count the empty fields in column 6, as on the AWK page, and look at which strains they belong to:

awk -F'\t' '$6 == ""' growth_genus.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' '$6 == "" { print $2 }' growth_genus.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
209
    209 mock
209 lines without a genus, all of them mock plants. That is expected: these plants got no bacteria. If other names show up here, a name did not match.
Check 2: strains that were not used. This time, read the growth data first and remember which strains it has. Then go through the metadata, and print the strains that were not seen in the growth data:

awk -F'\t' '
  NR == FNR                 { seen[$2] = 1; next }
  FNR > 1 && !($1 in seen)  { print $1 }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt mmc5_metadata_named.txt | wc -l

awk -F'\t' '
  NR == FNR                 { seen[$2] = 1; next }
  FNR > 1 && !($1 in seen)  { print $1 }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt mmc5_metadata_named.txt | head -3

This prints:
25

Root123D2
Root381
USDA61
Taken apart:

seen[$2] = 1: store the value 1 under the name of the strain in column 2 of the growth data. The value itself does not matter, any value would do. What matters is that after the first file, every strain of the growth data is a name in the array seen.
($1 in seen): true if the strain in column 1 of the metadata is a name in seen. in only looks at the names, not at the values.
! means “not”, so !($1 in seen) is true for the strains that were not seen. The brackets keep the test together, so that ! turns the whole test around.
FNR > 1 skips the header of the metadata.

25 of the 27 strains do not appear in the growth data. That is fine here, because the experiment used only two of them. In your own data, an entry you expected to be used may point to a name that is written differently in the two files. Without the !, the same command prints the strains that were used:

awk -F'\t' '
  NR == FNR                 { seen[$2] = 1; next }
  FNR > 1 && ($1 in seen)   { print $1 }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt mmc5_metadata_named.txt

This prints:
129E
13C
What the checks do not catch. Run the same join and checks with the general rule from the tip above (s/^R//; s/_//, which removes the R at the start and the underscore):

sed 's/^R//; s/_//' mmc5_metadata_fixed.txt > mmc5_metadata_wrong.txt

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  NR == FNR  { genus[$1] = $4; next }
  FNR == 1   { print $0, "Genus"; next }
             { print $0, genus[$2] }
' mmc5_metadata_wrong.txt awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > growth_genus_wrong.txt

# Check 1, and a comparison with the correct join
awk -F'\t' '$6 == "" { print $2 }' growth_genus_wrong.txt | sort | uniq -c
cmp growth_genus_wrong.txt growth_genus.txt && echo 'identical to the correct join'

# Check 2
awk -F'\t' '
  NR == FNR                 { seen[$2] = 1; next }
  FNR > 1 && !($1 in seen)  { print $1 }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt mmc5_metadata_wrong.txt | head -3

This prints:
    209 mock
identical to the correct join
oot123D2
oot381
USDA61
The join is exactly the same as with the correct names, because 129E and 13C still match. But the metadata is now broken: 17 strains lost their R. Check 1 cannot see this. Check 2 shows it, but only if you read the names it prints.
The checks give you numbers and names. Whether they show a problem, you decide: 209 mock plants without a genus is expected, a strain called oot123D2 is not.






TipTip: joins in other tools (optional)





AWK is not the only way to combine two tables. In bash, there is also the join command, and in R you would use left_join() from the dplyr package, or merge(). An LLM may suggest any of these. They look different, but they do the same job: match the lines of two tables by a shared name.
So the checks on this page still apply. Make the names match first, then count the lines, look at the lines without a match and see which names they belong to, and look for entries that were not used. Tools differ in what they do with a name that has no match: some leave an empty field, as AWK does, and others leave out the line. Then the line count is the check that catches it.









QuestionExercise





The mock plants got an empty field in the new column. But their genus is not unknown: they got no bacteria at all. Write a second command that puts the text none into column 6 of the mock plants, and leaves all other lines as they are. Use growth_genus.txt as input, save the result as growth_genus_none.txt, and check it.
Hint: on the sed page, you changed column 2 on some lines only, with a pattern, an action and { print }.






AnswerClick me to see an answer





The pattern $2 == "mock" picks the mock plants, and the action puts none into column 6. The second part, { print }, prints every line, changed or not. -v OFS='\t' keeps the tabs in the lines that changed:

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '$2 == "mock" { $6 = "none" } { print }' growth_genus.txt > growth_genus_none.txt

# Check
wc -l growth_genus_none.txt
head -3 growth_genus_none.txt
awk -F'\t' '$6 == ""' growth_genus_none.txt | wc -l
cut -f2,6 growth_genus_none.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
595 growth_genus_none.txt

Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg Genus
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6 none
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8 none

0

    210 129E    Rhizobium
    175 13C Rhizobium
      1 Condition   Genus
    209 mock    none
No empty fields are left, and each condition got the value you expected. Note that the command only changes the mock plants. A strain whose name does not match still gets an empty field, so check 1 still finds it. If you filled in every empty field instead, a name that did not match would look the same as a mock plant.

title: Combining two files
section: Windows line endings in a join
text:
Windows line endings in a join
On the sed page, you removed the hidden \r from the metadata before you used it. Here is what happens if you skip that step. The \r sits at the end of each line, so it is part of the last column, column 12 (Colonization). Add this column to the growth data, once from the clean file and once from a renamed copy of the original Windows file:

# The Windows file, with the two names changed, but without removing the \r
sed 's/^R129_E/129E/; s/^R13_C/13C/' awk_data/mmc5_metadata.txt > mmc5_metadata_named_windows.txt

# Add column 12, from the clean file and from the Windows file
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  NR == FNR  { colon[$1] = $12; next }
  FNR == 1   { print $0, "Colonization"; next }
             { print $0, colon[$2] }
' mmc5_metadata_named.txt awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > growth_colon.txt

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  NR == FNR  { colon[$1] = $12; next }
  FNR == 1   { print $0, "Colonization"; next }
             { print $0, colon[$2] }
' mmc5_metadata_named_windows.txt awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > growth_colon_windows.txt

# Count the plants with TRUE in the new column, and look at one line
awk -F'\t' '$6 == "TRUE"' growth_colon.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' '$6 == "TRUE"' growth_colon_windows.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' '$2 == "129E"' growth_colon_windows.txt | head -1 | cat -A

This prints:
210
0
low_P^I129E^Iex61^I86.1^I5.5^ITRUE^M$
The \r (^M) came along with the value, so the next command that looks for TRUE finds nothing. If you add column 4 (the genus) from the Windows file instead, the result is exactly the same as from the clean file, because the \r is not in column 4. So a file with Windows line endings can work fine in one join and quietly break the next one. Remove the \r before you combine files, as on the sed page.






ImportantGit Bash hides this problem



In Git Bash on Windows, AWK drops the \r when it reads the file. There, the join with the Windows file gives exactly the same result as with the clean one, and you find 210 plants with TRUE. On Linux, for example on a computer cluster, you find 0. Check new files with file or cat -A before you combine them, whatever system you work on.








QuestionExercise






Add two columns from the metadata to the growth data in one command: the genus (column 4) and Colonization (column 12). Give both new columns a name in the header. Save the result as growth_meta.txt.
Check the result: the number of lines, the number of fields per line, and which values of Colonization each condition got.







AnswerClick me to see an answer





Use one array per column you want to add:

# 1. Two arrays, and two new columns
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  NR == FNR  { genus[$1] = $4; colon[$1] = $12; next }
  FNR == 1   { print $0, "Genus", "Colonization"; next }
             { print $0, genus[$2], colon[$2] }
' mmc5_metadata_named.txt awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > growth_meta.txt

# 2. Check
wc -l growth_meta.txt
head -3 growth_meta.txt
awk -F'\t' '{ print NF }' growth_meta.txt | sort | uniq -c
cut -f2,7 growth_meta.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
595 growth_meta.txt

Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg Genus   Colonization
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8

    595 7

    210 129E    TRUE
    175 13C NA
      1 Condition   Colonization
    209 mock
All 595 lines have 7 fields. 129E got TRUE, 13C got the text NA, and the mock plants got nothing. Note that the table now holds two kinds of missing values: the text NA from the metadata, and empty fields for the mock plants. When you calculate with such a column, you need the rule from the AWK page for both.

title: Combining two files
text:
What you learned

A join adds information from one table to another, using a name that both tables share.
Before a join, look at the names in both files. They must match letter by letter.
Make names match with explicit changes (s/^R129_E/129E/), and check all names afterwards, not only the ones you changed. Choose one naming scheme early in a project, so you need this less often.
NR == FNR { genus[$1] = $4; next } { print $0, genus[$2] } combines two files: the table you look things up in first, the table you add to second. FNR == 1 gives the new column a name.
NR counts lines across all files, FNR within the current file. next skips the rest of the command for the current line.
A missing name gives an empty field, not an error. After a join, count the lines, count the empty fields and see which names they belong to, and look for entries that were not used. Read the names these checks print, not only the counts.
A Windows line ending travels into your result when you add the last column. Remove it before the join.

The next page, AWK and sed on FASTA files, is optional. It uses AWK and sed on sequence files. After it, Checking code from an LLM puts the checks from all pages together.

title: AWK on a table
text:
On this page, you use AWK on a real table with plant growth measurements. You choose columns, keep the rows you need, add a new column, and calculate means per group. Along the way, you meet the most common trap when you work with tables: missing values that quietly change your results.
The same commands work on any table in plain text, and many bioinformatics tools write their results that way, for example BLAST, featureCounts or a GFF annotation file. With AWK you can filter or reshape such output right away, or pass it on to the next tool with a pipe, without saving it first or opening it in R. AWK never changes the file it reads: it prints the result on the screen, or into a new file if you ask for that.

title: AWK on a table
section: Get the data: curl and tar
text:
Get the data: curl and tar
All example files for this tutorial come in one file, awk_data.tar.gz. A .tar.gz file packs many files into one and compresses them, similar to a .zip file.

# Go to your home folder, and make a folder for this tutorial
cd ~
mkdir awk_tutorial
cd awk_tutorial

# Download the data
# -L: if the link sends you on to another address, follow it
# -O: save the file under its own name, awk_data.tar.gz
curl -L -O "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ndombrowski/AWK_tutorial/main/data/awk_data.tar.gz"

# Unpack it. Used options:
# -x extract, -z it is compressed (.gz), -f the file name follows
tar -xzf awk_data.tar.gz

# Check: you should see awk_data and awk_data.tar.gz
ls

# Check: you should see 14 files
ls awk_data
ls awk_data | wc -l

On this page you only need Growth_Data.txt. The other files are 16S sequences, a table with information on bacterial strains, and a second version of the growth table, which you use on later pages.

title: AWK on a table
text:
Look at the table first
Before you run any command on a table, you want to look at it first. You at least want to know: how many lines it has, and what separates the columns?

# The first 5 lines
head -5 awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# The number of lines
wc -l awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8
low_P   mock    ex61    74.7    8.1
low_P   mock    ex61    34.4    8.3

595 awk_data/Growth_Data.txt
You see that the table has a header, a first line with the column names followed by 594 rows of measurements. Each row is one plant that was measured, and the table has the following columns:

Nutrient: the plant grew with low or high phosphorus (low_P, high_P)
Condition: the plant was inoculated with nothing (mock) or with one of two bacteria (129E, 13C)
Experiment: the experiment the plant was part of (ex61, ex64, ex65)
Rootlength: root length in mm
FW_shoot_mg: shoot fresh weight in mg

The columns look like they are separated by spaces. However, you cannot see what is really there, because spaces and tabs look the same on screen. cat -A shows the invisible characters:

head -3 awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | cat -A

This prints:
Nutrient^ICondition^IExperiment^IRootlength^IFW_shoot_mg$
low_P^Imock^Iex61^I40.4^I6.6$
low_P^Imock^Iex61^I38^I6.8$
Here, ^I is a tab, and $ marks the end of each line. So this tells you that you work with a tab-separated table. You need to know this for the next steps.






TipTip: cat -A on a Mac (optional)






On a Mac, cat -A may not work and you can try cat -et instead.

title: AWK on a table
section: The shape of an AWK command
text:
The shape of an AWK command
Every AWK command on this page has the same shape:
awk -F'\t' 'pattern { action }' file

-F'\t' tells AWK that the columns are separated by tabs. -F stands for field separator. A field is one value in a line, like one cell in a spreadsheet row.
'pattern { action }' is the AWK program, it always needs to be between single quotes. The pattern says which lines to work on. The action, between curly brackets, says what to do with them.
file is the file AWK reads.

AWK reads the file one line at a time. For each line, it checks the pattern. If the line matches, AWK runs the action. You can leave out either part: without a pattern, the action runs on every line. Without an action, AWK prints the lines that match.

title: AWK on a table
text:
print: choose columns
AWK gives each field of a line a number: $1 is the first field, $2 the second, and so on. $0 is the whole line. To print the first column:

# Print column 1 of every line, and show the first 3 lines of the result
awk -F'\t' '{ print $1 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient
low_P
low_P
To print several columns, separate the fields you want with a comma:

# Print column 1 (Nutrient) and column 4 (Rootlength)
awk -F'\t' '{ print $1, $4 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient Rootlength
low_P 40.4
low_P 38
AWK by default puts a space between the printed columns. To keep the result a tab-separated table, tell AWK to use a tab in the output too. -v OFS='\t' sets the output field separator:

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '{ print $1, $4 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
Nutrient    Rootlength
low_P   40.4
low_P   38
You can do the same thing with cut -f1,4 (something you might have seen in the CLI workshop). However, you will see why AWK becomes more useful in the next sections, where you choose rows too.

title: AWK on a table
section: NF: work with the number of fields
text:
NF: work with the number of fields
Before that, you learn a quick check that is useful for any table you work with: count the fields in each line. Here, NF is the number of fields in the current line:

# Count the fields per line, then count how often each number occurs
awk -F'\t' '{ print NF }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
    595 5
This tells you that all 595 lines have 5 fields. If some lines had 4 or 6, this would immediately tell you that something in the table would be off. So this is a quick command to check that your data has the right structure.






QuestionExercise






Print the columns Experiment and FW_shoot_mg, separated by a tab. Look at the first 4 lines of the result.







AnswerClick me to see an answer





Experiment is column 3 and FW_shoot_mg is column 5:

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '{ print $3, $5 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -4

This prints:
Experiment  FW_shoot_mg
ex61    6.6
ex61    6.8
ex61    8.1

title: AWK on a table
section: NR: work with the header line
text:
NR: work with the header line
NR is the number of the record, the line AWK is reading now. You can use it in a pattern to choose lines by their position:

# Only line 1, the header
awk -F'\t' 'NR == 1' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# All lines after the header: show the first 2, and count them
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -2
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8

594
These commands have only a pattern and no action, so AWK prints the lines that match. NR > 1 skips the header and keeps all 594 rows of data. You need it often, as you will see in the next sections.

title: AWK on a table
text:
Subset rows by text
Sometimes you only care about part of the data. For example, you might want to keep only the plants grown with low phosphorus. For this, you use the pattern $1 == "low_P", which checks every line and keeps it only if column 1 is exactly low_P. The first command shows the first few matching lines. The second counts how many rows you now work with:

awk -F'\t' '$1 == "low_P"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3
awk -F'\t' '$1 == "low_P"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8
low_P   mock    ex61    74.7    8.1

300
Two details matter here:

Text goes between double quotes: "low_P". Without quotes, AWK reads low_P as the name of a variable, a name that holds a value, like a label on a box. You never gave low_P a value, so it is empty, and no row matches.
To compare, use two equal signs: ==. If you use only one equal sign, this command does something else and instead puts a value into a field. Note here how AWK gives you no error message. Only by looking at the output, and counting the number of lines of the output, do you see that the command does something different from what you wanted:


# Wrong: one = instead of two
awk -F'\t' '$1 = "low_P"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3
awk -F'\t' '$1 = "low_P"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
low_P Condition Experiment Rootlength FW_shoot_mg
low_P mock ex61 40.4 6.6
low_P mock ex61 38 6.8

595
You see that with this command every line is kept, but column 1 of every line now says low_P, even in the header, and the tabs became spaces. A quick wc -l shows the problem: 595 lines, the same as the whole file.

Why not use grep?
If you have followed the CLI workshop you might remember grep, which keeps lines that contain a word. If you wanted to only work with the plants with bacterium 13C, both tools give the same count:

grep '13C' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' '$2 == "13C"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
175
175
But there is an important difference: grep searches the whole line, not one column. This can easily result in problems, for example if you would have searched for 13 instead of 13C:

grep '13' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
grep '13' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
211

low_P   mock    ex61    55.3    13.3
low_P   mock    ex61    48.7    13.9
low_P   mock    ex64    46.93   13.52
In total this command gives you 36 extra lines. That is because 13 also appears in shoot weights such as 13.3. You see this in the first lines grep finds that are not even 13C plants, but mock plants with such a shoot weight. In contrast, AWK compares only column 2, so this cannot happen. This makes the AWK command much safer.

title: AWK on a table
text:
Subset rows by a number
Comparisons also work with numbers: > (greater than), < (less than), >= and <= (greater or less than, or equal). For example, you could only keep plants with roots longer than 50 mm:

awk -F'\t' '$4 > 50' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3
awk -F'\t' '$4 > 50' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg
low_P   mock    ex61    74.7    8.1
low_P   mock    ex61    66.5    8.9

476
Important: Note how the header is in the result? This might seem weird, since column 4 of the header is the word Rootlength, not a number. However, when a value is not a number, AWK compares it as text, and in that comparison Rootlength counts as larger than 50. To avoid this, add NR > 1 to skip the header. To combine patterns, use &&, which means “and”: both conditions must be true.

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 > 50' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
475
You sometimes might also need ||, which means means “or”: use this if you want at least one of the conditions to be true.
