# Low phosphorus and no bacteria
awk -F'\t' '$1 == "low_P" && $2 == "mock"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# Either of the two bacteria
awk -F'\t' '$2 == "129E" || $2 == "13C"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt







QuestionExercise






How many plants grew with high phosphorus and bacterium 13C?
How many plants have a shoot weight above 20 mg?







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# 1. Two text conditions with &&
awk -F'\t' '$1 == "high_P" && $2 == "13C"' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

# 2. NR > 1 keeps the header out
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $5 > 20' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
87

140
So 87 plants grew with high phosphorus and 13C, and 140 plants have a shoot weight above 20 mg.

title: AWK on a table
section: Working with missing values: empty fields
text:
Working with missing values: empty fields
Next let’s look at one example to showcase why it is important to carefully check your data. For this, look for plants with very short roots, below 10 mm:

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 < 10' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 < 10' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
15

high_P  mock    ex61        18.2
high_P  mock    ex64        22.4
high_P  mock    ex64        26
This tells you that there seem to be 15 plants with short shoots. However, if you look at the table, you notice that none of them actually has a root length below 10. Instead, these rows have no root length at all. cat -A shows you exactly what is in the file for these fields:

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 < 10' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3 | cat -A

This prints:
high_P^Imock^Iex61^I^I18.2$
high_P^Imock^Iex64^I^I22.4$
high_P^Imock^Iex64^I^I26$
You see two tabs side by side, ^I^I, with nothing between them: this is an empty field and also how a missing value often looks, for example in a table saved from Excel with empty cells. Now count how many empty fields each column has:

# Empty root length (column 4) and empty shoot weight (column 5)
awk -F'\t' '$4 == ""' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' '$5 == ""' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
15
8
Altogether, this tells you that AWK did not give an error, but it did something you didn’t really want. It compared the empty field with 10 as text, and empty text counts as smaller than anything. So all 15 plants without a root length passed the filter $4 < 10. In calculations, AWK will treat an empty field as 0, as you see further down.






ImportantImportant: skip empty fields before you compare or calculate



Before you compare or calculate with a column, keep only the rows that have a value in it, with $4 != "". != means “is not equal to”, and "" is empty text, so $4 != "" means “column 4 is not empty”:

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 != "" && $4 < 10' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
0
No plant in this table has roots shorter than 10 mm.



Why -F'\t' matters
AWK can also run without -F'\t'. It then splits lines at any run of spaces and tabs. For most lines in this table, the result is the same. But AWK then treats the two tabs around an empty field as one separator, and the values move one column to the left. Line 123 is the first row with an empty root length:

# Line 123, and its column 4 with -F'\t'
awk -F'\t' 'NR == 123' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt
awk -F'\t' 'NR == 123 { print $4 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# Column 4 of the same line without -F'\t'
awk 'NR == 123 { print $4 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# Number of fields per line without -F'\t'
awk '{ print NF }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
high_P  mock    ex61        18.2

18.2

     23 4
    572 5
With -F'\t', column 4 of line 123 is empty (the empty line in the output). Without it, column 4 is 18.2, the shoot weight. The 23 lines with an empty field now have only 4 fields. Again there is no error. The NF check from above shows the problem right away, so it is worth running on every new table.
The count tells you that 23 lines are different, but not which ones. To find them, use NF as a pattern: NF != 5 keeps only the lines that do not have 5 fields. print NR, $0 prints the line number in front of each line:

# Which lines do not have 5 fields without -F'\t'?
awk 'NF != 5 { print NR, $0 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | head -3

This prints:
33 low_P    mock    ex61    49.6
34 low_P    mock    ex61    53.6
123 high_P  mock    ex61        18.2
Lines 33 and 34 have no shoot weight, and line 123 has no root length. Together, the 15 empty root lengths and 8 empty shoot weights make the 23 lines. On a new table, the line numbers tell you where to look, for example with awk 'NR == 33'.






QuestionExercise






How many plants have a shoot weight below 5 mg? First write the command without the rule from above. Then add the rule. What is the difference, and why?







AnswerClick me to see an answer






# Without the rule
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $5 < 5' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

# With the rule: skip empty shoot weights
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $5 != "" && $5 < 5' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | wc -l

This prints:
10
2
Only 2 plants have a shoot weight below 5 mg. The first command also keeps the 8 plants without a shoot weight.












TipTip: fill empty fields with NA (optional)





Empty fields are easy to miss. One way to make them visible is to fill each empty field with NA (not available) and save the result as a new file. In this table, only column 4 and column 5 have empty fields, so you fill those two:

# If column 4 is empty, put NA into it.
# If column 5 is empty, put NA into it.
# Then print every line.
# The command is spread over several lines to make it easier to read
# (more on this in "Add a column" below).
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  $4 == "" { $4 = "NA" }
  $5 == "" { $5 = "NA" }
  { print }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > Growth_Data_NA.txt

# Check: same number of lines, and line 123 now has NA
wc -l Growth_Data_NA.txt
awk -F'\t' 'NR == 123' Growth_Data_NA.txt

This prints:
595 Growth_Data_NA.txt
high_P  mock    ex61    NA  18.2
Also here -v OFS='\t' matters. When you change a field, AWK rebuilds the whole line and puts the output separator between the fields. Without -v OFS='\t', that is a space. Only the changed lines get spaces, the others keep their tabs, so the file now mixes both. cat -A shows this for line 123 (changed) and line 2 (not changed) of such a file:
high_P mock ex61 NA 18.2$
low_P^Imock^Iex61^I40.4^I6.6$
If you do not know which columns have empty fields, or there are many columns, you can let AWK go through all fields with a loop. You do not need to remember this form. Keep it in your notes, or ask an LLM for it and check the result as shown here. In this table it gives exactly the same file:

# For each field in the line (i = 1 up to the number of fields NF):
# if the field is empty, put NA into it. Then print the line.
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  {
    for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) {
      if ($i == "") { $i = "NA" }
    }
    print
  }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

Now the missing values are visible when you look at the file. Also, the columns no longer shift in tools that split at spaces and tabs, such as AWK without -F'\t', or join and column -t with their default settings.
But when you do this, it’s important to know that NA does not make comparisons safe. NA is text too, and in a text comparison it counts as larger than 50:

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 > 50' Growth_Data_NA.txt | wc -l
awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $4 != "NA" && $4 > 50' Growth_Data_NA.txt | wc -l

This prints:
490
475
So with NA, the rule stays the same, only with $4 != "NA" instead of $4 != "".

title: AWK on a table
text:
Add a column
AWK can calculate with fields. For example, the shoot weight per mm of root is $5 / $4. To add it as a new column at the end of each line, print the whole line $0 and then the result:

awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' 'NR > 1 { print $0, $5 / $4 }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > shoot_per_root.txt

wc -l shoot_per_root.txt

This prints:
awk: cmd. line:1: (FILENAME=awk_data/Growth_Data.txt FNR=123) fatal: division by zero attempted
121 shoot_per_root.txt
The error message tells you that AWK stopped at line 123: the first row with an empty root length. That is because it treated the empty field as 0, and a division by 0 is not possible. The file shoot_per_root.txt still exists, but it has only 121 lines instead of 594. If you missed the error message and only looked at head, the file would look fine. This is why you want to make it a habit to count lines after each step.
To fix this, you need to skip rows with an empty root length or shoot weight, and print a header for the new column. The command now has two parts, each with its own pattern and action.
A command with several parts gets long on one line. AWK lets you spread the part between the single quotes over several lines, so you can put each pattern and its action on a line of its own. The command does exactly the same, it is only easier to read. You can copy it into your terminal as it is: the terminal waits for the closing quote before it runs the command.

# Part 1: on line 1, print the current header and add a name for the new column
# Part 2: on the other lines with both values, print the line plus the result
awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '
  NR == 1                          { print $0, "shoot_per_root" }
  NR > 1 && $4 != "" && $5 != ""   { print $0, $5 / $4 }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt > shoot_per_root.txt

# Check the result
head -3 shoot_per_root.txt
wc -l shoot_per_root.txt

This prints:
Nutrient    Condition   Experiment  Rootlength  FW_shoot_mg shoot_per_root
low_P   mock    ex61    40.4    6.6 0.163366
low_P   mock    ex61    38  6.8 0.178947

572 shoot_per_root.txt
572 lines: the header plus 571 plants. Does that add up? 594 plants, minus 15 without a root length, minus 8 without a shoot weight, is 571. No plant misses both values, so no row is subtracted twice.






ImportantKeep the opening brace on the same line as its pattern



When you spread a command over several lines, the opening { of an action must stay on the same line as its pattern. If you move the { to the next line, AWK reads the pattern on its own (which prints every matching line) and the action on its own (which runs on every line). You get no error, only a different result.

title: AWK on a table
section: Sum and mean of a column: variables and END
text:
Sum and mean of a column: variables and END
You will notice that the commands from here on are longer than the ones before. You could do the same thing in R or Python, and you might wonder why even learn them in AWK? The reason is that in bioinformatics you often only need a quick look at your data: what is the total number of reads I work with, how many plants are in each group, and do the means look sensible? AWK gives you that answer in the terminal, without starting another program or loading the table first. On a computer cluster, where R or Python may not be set up for you, AWK is always there. And because AWK reads a file one line at a time, it also works on files that are too large to open comfortably in R or Excel. For statistics and plots, R or Python remain the better tools. AWK is for the quick check before, or for cleaning up a table before you load it there.
Start with one number: the total shoot weight of all plants. For this, AWK needs a variable, a name that holds a value. You do not need to create it first: AWK makes the variable the first time you use it, and it starts at 0.

awk -F'\t' 'NR > 1 && $5 != "" { sum += $5 } END { print sum }' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
9715.23
Taken apart:

sum += $5: add the shoot weight of this line to the variable sum. += means “add to the value that is already in sum”.
END { print sum }: END is a special pattern. Its action runs once, after AWK has read the last line. By then, sum holds the total.

The name sum is your own choice. You could call it total or weight instead, and get the same result. Names such as NR, NF and END are different: they belong to AWK and have a fixed meaning.
For the mean, you need a second variable that counts the number of plants measured. Here it is called n (short for “number of plants”), and n++ adds 1 to it for each line AWK passed. The ; separates two steps inside one action:

awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 && $5 != "" { sum += $5; n++ }
  END                { print n, sum, sum / n }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints the number of plants, the total and the mean:
586 9715.23 16.5789
When you run such calculations, you want to check if 586 adds up: 594 plants, minus the 8 without a shoot weight, is 586.
Now leave out the rule for empty fields, and then also NR > 1 to see how slight differences in the code can make a difference:

# Without $5 != ""
awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 { sum += $5; n++ }
  END    { print n, sum, sum / n }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# Also without NR > 1
awk -F'\t' '
  { sum += $5; n++ }
  END { print n, sum, sum / n }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
594 9715.23 16.3556

595 9715.23 16.3281
The total is the same all three times. AWK adds an empty field as 0, and the header text FW_shoot_mg as 0 too, so the sum does not change. But n still counts these lines, so the mean drops. A mean that looks right does not mean that it is actually right. This is a good example to carefully think about what your code is doing since the code runs without any error but the output is still incorrect. In this case the difference is small, but depending on your data, such silent errors can have a large effect.
The means above have more decimals than the measurements. To round them, use printf instead of print. printf prints with a format that you choose: a piece of text with placeholders that the values fill in order. %d stands for a whole number and %.1f for a number with one decimal. \t is a tab and \n a new line. Everything else in the format, such as n: and mean:, is printed as it is:

awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 && $5 != "" { sum += $5; n++ }
  END                { printf "n: %d\tmean: %.1f\n", n, sum / n }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
n: 586  mean: 16.6
Unlike print, printf does not start a new line by itself, and it ignores OFS. Leave out the \n, and the prompt of your terminal ends up on the same line as the result. The tab between the values is there only because \t is in the format.

title: AWK on a table
section: Count and mean per group: arrays
text:
Count and mean per group: arrays
sum and n are single variables: each holds one value for the whole file. You can do more than that, for example count the plants per nutrient level. For this, you need one count per group. An array is a variable that holds one value per name. n["low_P"] is the count for low_P, and n["high_P"] the count for high_P. Just like a single variable, AWK makes the value for a new name the first time you use it, and it starts at 0.

awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 { n[$1]++ }
  END    { for (group in n) { print group, n[group] } }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
low_P 300

high_P 294
Taken apart:

NR > 1 { n[$1]++ }: for each row of data, add 1 to the count of its nutrient level. Piece by piece:

n is the name of the array.
[$1] picks one name in the array: the text in column 1. On a low_P row that is n["low_P"].
++ adds 1 to the value under that name.

So after the first low_P row, n["low_P"] is 1, after the second it is 2, and so on.
END { ... }: as before, this runs once, after the last line.
for (group in n) { print group, n[group] }: go through all names in n. For each name, put it into the variable group, and print the name and its count.

You can check the result with tools from the CLI workshop:

cut -f1 awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | sort | uniq -c

This prints:
      1 Nutrient
    294 high_P
    300 low_P
To calculate the mean per group, you do the same as for the whole file, but with two arrays: sum for the sum per group and n for the count per group. sum[$1] += $4 adds the root length to the sum of its group.

# Without the rule for empty fields
awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 { sum[$1] += $4; n[$1]++ }
  END    { for (group in sum) { print group, n[group], sum[group] / n[group] } }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

# With the rule: skip empty root lengths
awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 && $4 != "" { sum[$1] += $4; n[$1]++ }
  END                { for (group in sum) { print group, n[group], sum[group] / n[group] } }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt

This prints:
low_P 300 57.9494
high_P 294 88.9501

low_P 290 59.9477
high_P 289 90.489
Without the rule, AWK adds 0 for each empty root length and still counts the plant. This is another silent error: both means come out too low, and nothing warns you.

Mean per nutrient and condition
To group data by more than one column, you can glue the columns together into one name: $1"-"$2 is column 1, a dash and column 2, for example low_P-mock. The dash goes in double quotes, because it is text here. A dash appears in none of the values, so you can split the name again later if you need to.

awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 && $4 != "" { group = $1"-"$2; sum[group] += $4; n[group]++ }
  END                { for (group in sum) { printf "%s\t%d\t%.1f\n", group, n[group], sum[group] / n[group] } }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | sort

This prints:
high_P-129E 103 98.4
high_P-13C  85  97.7
high_P-mock 101 76.4
low_P-129E  99  69.9
low_P-13C   86  64.2
low_P-mock  105 47.1
Taken apart:

printf with the format "%s\t%d\t%.1f\n": the group name, a tab, the count as a whole number, a tab, and the mean with one decimal. %s is new: it stands for text, here the group name.
| sort: AWK goes through the names in an array in no fixed order. Sort the result, so that it is easy to read and to compare between runs.







ImportantForget the quotes, and the dash becomes a minus



If you write group = $1-$2 without the quotes, AWK reads the dash as a minus and subtracts column 2 from column 1. Text that does not start with a number counts as 0, so low_P and high_P both become 0, and 129E becomes 129. The command runs without an error, but prints this:
-129    202 84.4
-13 171 80.8
0   206 61.5
Three groups instead of six, and low_P and high_P plants mixed together. A quick check catches it: you expect 2 nutrient levels × 3 conditions = 6 groups, so count the lines of the output, and look at the group names.


Without the rule $4 != "", four of the six means are lower. For example, low_P with 129E gives 64.7 instead of 69.9, because the 8 plants without a root length count as 0 mm.






QuestionExercise






Calculate the mean shoot weight per Condition, with one decimal. How many plants are in each group?







AnswerClick me to see an answer





Condition is column 2, and the shoot weight is column 5. Skip the empty shoot weights:

awk -F'\t' '
  NR > 1 && $5 != "" { sum[$2] += $5; n[$2]++ }
  END                { for (group in sum) { printf "%s\t%d\t%.1f\n", group, n[group], sum[group] / n[group] } }
' awk_data/Growth_Data.txt | sort

This prints:
129E    208 17.6
13C 173 15.3
mock    205 16.6

title: AWK on a table
text:
What you learned

An AWK command has the shape awk -F'\t' 'pattern { action }' file.
$1, $2, … are the fields of a line, $0 the whole line, NF the number of fields, NR the line number.
Compare with ==, !=, >, <, and combine with && (and) and || (or). Text goes in double quotes.
A variable (sum += $5) and END give a total or a mean for the whole file; an array (sum[$1] += $5) gives one per group.
Look at the table first: cat -A for tabs and empty fields, NF for the number of fields per line.
Empty fields cause errors without a warning: skip them with $4 != "" before you compare or calculate.
After each step, check the result: count the lines, and look at it with head.

You do not need to learn these commands by heart. Instead, keep your own notes: a text file or notebook with the commands you have checked, each with one line on what it does and which trap it avoids (for example “skips empty fields in column 4”). A checked command in your notes is worth more than one you half remember, and more than a new one from an LLM that you still have to check.
On the next page, sed basics, you change text in a file: search and replace, delete lines, and clean up a file with Windows line endings.
